claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by configurational-entropy stabilization.
Configurational entropy promotes a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
Adding elements while retaining near-equiatomic ratios increases nanoparticle configurational entropy.
The proposed stability mechanism applies during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
The proposed stability mechanism applies during thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
Reducing the driving force for phase separation maintains a single-phase solid solution at high temperature.
Maintaining the single-phase solid solution prevents chemical instability at high temperature.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoparticles will resist phase segregation better than lower-entropy counterparts under identical conditions.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoparticles will resist chemical degradation better than lower-entropy counterparts under identical conditions.
Nanoparticles with fewer elements and lower configurational entropy are expected to undergo more phase segregation.
Nanoparticles with fewer elements and lower configurational entropy are expected to undergo more chemical instability.
The hypothesis is restricted to systems whose enthalpy of mixing is not overwhelmingly positive.
A sufficiently positive enthalpy of mixing can overcome entropy stabilization.
A near-equiatomic alloy containing five or more elements can serve as the high-configurational-entropy test material.
A near-equiatomic three-element alloy can serve as the lower-configurational-entropy control.
